planting.note: Plant whole cormels 3-4 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil once the ground has warmed; this is the pale-fleshed, mild-flavored malanga clone most commonly sold fresh in Caribbean and Latin markets, distinguished from other Xanthosoma color types by its white-to-cream corm flesh and relatively smooth skin.

directions: Plant cormels in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; this white-fleshed market type is a staple in Cuban, Dominican, and Puerto Rican cooking, prized for a milder, starchier result than purple or yellow malanga types when boiled, fried, or mashed. Keep soil evenly moist throughout the 8-11 month growing season and mulch heavily, since the shallow corm system dries out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils. Harvest once the lower leaves yellow and die back, usually after the first light frost knocks the foliage down in zone 9a. Always cook thoroughly before eating, as raw corms and leaves contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant tuber head-sets (the crown end, 3-6 oz with intact skin) 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed well past last frost; provide a sturdy 8-10 foot trellis immediately since vines climb fast and are heavy once laden with foliage.

directions: Grow this named Jamaican export-quality yam type on a tall, sturdy trellis in full sun and deep, well-drained, fertile soil mounded or ridged to ease harvest. Unlike the deep-purple-fleshed winged yam types already common in cultivation, the Lucea strain produces large, smooth-skinned tubers with firm, white to pale-yellow flesh prized for its dry, mealy texture when boiled or roasted. Water regularly during the long warm season but reduce irrigation as vines begin to yellow and die back near harvest, typically 9-12 months after planting in a zone 9a season extended with early spring planting and season-end curing. Store cured tubers in a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot out of direct sun.
sources: Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI)
Jamaica Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries - Bodles Research Station
